paragraphs: The core of this work is not the vague notion of 'knowing people', but winning opportunities for clients within the scope of their authorisation, settling the terms clearly, and maintaining checkable contracts and files. Judging fit should rely on observable task behaviour and working conditions, not personality labels; the exercises and checklists on this page were designed by the editors from public occupational sources for self-exploration, and do not constitute criteria for hiring, screening or ability assessment.

A stronger signal is: you are willing to maintain client relationships proactively, can explain the boundaries of your authority clearly in negotiations, can coordinate the schedules of several parties at once, and stop and escalate when the authorisation is unclear or a payment looks wrong. A single mock client and opportunity-screening exercise with a debrief record can test this: whether constraints were clarified, whether the quote is reproducible, and whether anomalies were closed out.

If you are unwilling to face clients and repeated rejection, find the intensity of schedules and travel hard to accept, tend to overlook contract and file details, or are not used to stopping and escalating when the authorisation is unclear, this kind of work may steadily drain you; job design varies considerably across organisations (performance agencies, sports agencies, artist studios), so first test your performance and tolerance with one complete opportunity-screening and contract-terms exercise.
Assessments and exercises serve only as a reference for self-exploration, and cannot predict hiring, competence or future performance.
